analysis.one_liner: Taxes hedge-fund and private-equity managers' carried interest as ordinary income instead of low-taxed gains.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Managers at private equity, hedge fund, and real estate investment partnerships are paid with 'carried interest' — a share of fund profits. Under current law that pay can be taxed at the lower capital-gains rate and postponed until the fund realizes its gains. This bill would tax that pay every year as ordinary income, subject to payroll taxes, and end the deferral. It never left the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers who bear a share of federal spending; the bill shifts a larger tax burden onto the highest-earning fund managers, some of whom make nine-figure incomes while paying capital-gains rates on their labor income.

how_it_helps.text: Requires partners to include a 'deemed compensation amount' in gross income annually as ordinary income, rather than treating their service-based partnership share as low-taxed capital gain.
Subjects that compensation to self-employment (payroll) taxation, which carried interest largely avoids.
Eliminates the ability to defer tax until the partnership realizes income, so managers pay as their compensation accrues rather than years later.
Repeals section 1061, the existing three-year holding-period rule that was the 2017 compromise on carried interest, replacing it with the stricter ordinary-income regime.

Includes anti-abuse rules: an 'applicable loan' definition with a safe harbor to stop partners borrowing from the fund to create fake invested capital, plus regulations targeting undervaluation, tiered structures, and income shifting to tax-indifferent parties.

analysis.who_pays: Fund managers at private equity, hedge funds, venture capital, and real estate investment partnerships, who would pay ordinary income and payroll tax rates on their performance pay and pay it sooner.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: Managers' performance pay is tied to fund profits that may not materialize; taxing a deemed amount annually, before the fund actually sells its investments, could force tax payments on paper income in years when the manager receives little or no cash.

The bill applies to real estate held for rental or investment, so it would reach not only hedge funds but real estate partnerships, and its formula (a specified rate plus 9 percentage points applied to invested capital) is complex and would require extensive Treasury regulations to administer.

Opponents have long argued that carried interest rewards long-term, at-risk investment and that taxing it as ordinary income raises the cost of capital for funds investing in startups, housing, and infrastructure; that objection is not resolved in the sources provided.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a large tax cut that currently goes to a few thousand of the highest-paid people in the country would end, and their labor-type income would be taxed like a nurse's or engineer's. The main honest cost is timing and complexity — managers could owe tax on profits they have not yet been paid, and the deemed-compensation formula adds administrative burden for funds of all sizes, including real estate partnerships. On balance the bill targets a widely criticized asymmetry in the tax code, though its one-size formula is blunt.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Wyden introduced the bill on November 15, 2023, with nine cosponsors including Sens. Whitehouse, King, Warren, Sanders, Schatz, Reed, Hirono, Markey, and Fetterman.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action appears in the bill's history — no committee markup, no floor vote, no House counterpart action — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate fund managers keep the current capital-gains treatment and deferral of their carried-interest pay, and the Treasury does not collect the additional revenue the bill would have raised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fund managers keeping their low tax rates

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tax carried interest as ordinary income and end deferral.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Private equity and hedge fund industry
against.role: Fund managers who benefit from carried-interest treatment
against.what_they_did: The industry has consistently lobbied against carried-interest tax increases; it did not need to act here because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters were Democrats or independents; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote where party lines would have been recorded.

industries.note: Managers' performance pay would be taxed annually at ordinary income and payroll tax rates instead of deferred capital-gains rates, ending a tax advantage worth billions a year to a small, highly paid group.
Hedge fund managers are the classic carried-interest beneficiaries; the bill removes their ability to convert service compensation into low-taxed gain and to defer tax.

The bill's definition of specified assets includes real estate held for rental or investment, so real estate fund managers are swept in; smaller partnerships would face compliance costs alongside the tax increase.
VC managers receive carried interest for raising and investing capital, which the bill's 'applicable trade or business' definition squarely covers.
